questions.q: What is the RMS value of a sinusoidal AC voltage whose peak value is 300 V? State the formula used and the final answer with units.
questions.a: Vrms = vm/√2 = 300 V / 1.414 ≈ 212 V. A wrong answer of 300 V reveals the student confuses peak value with RMS value. An answer of 150 V (300/2) reveals the student incorrectly uses 1/2 instead of 1/√2, confusing the average of sin²θ (which is 1/2) with the square root needed for RMS.

questions.q: The voltage across a household socket is rated as 220 V AC. A student says, "The voltage reaches 220 V at its peak." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not, and state what the actual peak voltage is.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The 220 V rating is the RMS value. The actual peak voltage is vm = √2 × Vrms = 1.414 × 220 V ≈ 311 V. A student who agrees with the statement does not understand that AC voltage ratings are universally given as RMS values (per NCERT Points to Ponder #1). This misconception leads to errors in calculating peak voltages for component ratings (e.g., capacitor voltage ratings, insulation breakdown).

questions.q: A 60 W incandescent bulb is designed for a 220 V RMS AC supply. Calculate: (a) the resistance of the bulb filament (assume constant), (b) the peak voltage across the filament, and (c) the RMS current through the bulb. Show all steps with units.
questions.a: (a) P = Vrms²/R → R = Vrms²/P = (220 V)² / 60 W = 48400 / 60 = 806.7 Ω. (b) vm = √2 × Vrms = 1.414 × 220 V = 311 V. (c) Irms = P/Vrms = 60 W / 220 V = 0.273 A. A common error: using peak voltage in P = V²/R gives R = (311)²/60 ≈ 1613 Ω (wrong by factor of 2). Another error: computing peak current as im = vm/R = 311/806.7 = 0.385 A but forgetting to convert to RMS (Irms = im/√2 = 0.273 A). Unit tracking: V²/W = V²/(V·A) = V/A = Ω ✓.

questions.q: Two AC sources produce sinusoidal voltages: Source A has vm = 200 V, Source B has Vrms = 150 V. Which source delivers more average power to an identical 100 Ω resistive load? Justify quantitatively.
questions.a: Source A: Vrms = 200/√2 ≈ 141.4 V → P = Vrms²/R = (141.4)²/100 = 200 W. Source B: Vrms = 150 V → P = (150)²/100 = 225 W. Source B delivers more power despite having a lower peak voltage (212 V vs 200 V). A student who chooses Source A because "200 > 150" is comparing peak voltage of A to RMS voltage of B — a unit/category mismatch. This tests whether the student recognizes that power depends on RMS values and that comparing peak to RMS is physically meaningless.

questions.q: A student solves Example 7.1 from NCERT (100 W bulb, 220 V supply) and writes: "Peak current im = P/vm = 100 W / 311 V = 0.322 A." Identify the error in this reasoning and provide the correct calculation for peak current.
questions.a: The error: P = VI holds for RMS values (P = Vrms Irms), not peak values. The student used peak voltage vm with average power P. Correct: Irms = P/Vrms = 100/220 = 0.455 A. Then im = √2 × Irms = 1.414 × 0.455 = 0.643 A. The student's answer (0.322 A) is exactly half the correct peak current because they effectively used P = vm im (missing the 1/2 factor from averaging sin²). This reveals confusion between instantaneous, peak, and RMS power relationships.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a resistor, an AC power supply (variable voltage), a DC power supply, and a thermometer to demonstrate that the RMS value of an AC voltage is the "equivalent DC voltage" for heating. Describe the procedure, measurements, and how you would verify Vrms = vm/√2.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Connect resistor to DC supply, adjust voltage Vdc until thermometer shows steady temperature rise ΔT after fixed time. Record Vdc. (2) Connect same resistor to AC supply, adjust peak voltage vm until same ΔT in same time. Record vm using oscilloscope. (3) Compute Vrms = vm/√2. (4) Verify Vdc ≈ Vrms. Expected outcome: Vdc = 10 V → vm ≈ 14.14 V. A poor answer would omit the oscilloscope measurement of vm, or use an AC voltmeter (which reads RMS directly) making the experiment circular. The key is independently measuring peak voltage and matching heating effects.
